clauses.reason: The only operative sentence of EO 8080 revokes the designation of Fair Haven, New York, as a customs port of entry in Customs Collection District No. 8 (Rochester), and a second sentence makes the order effective thirty days from the date of the order, which is April 4, 1939. Thirty days after April 4, 1939 is May 4, 1939, recorded as the date the revocation took effect. The order fixes no hour, so a reading that counts the thirty days differently could move the date by one day. The revocation is self-executing: it needed no further act by an official, so the command was exhausted by performance when it took effect. The surviving consequence is the removal of the port designation, a completed change and not a continuing command of this order.

research_rationale:
EO 8080 (April 4, 1939) revokes the designation of Fair Haven, New York, as a customs port of entry under the act of August 1, 1914 (38 Stat. 609, 623), effective thirty days from its date. I read the held text of the Federal Register page (4 FR 1475), which contains the whole order, its signature line, its date and its filing line, and compared the clause inventory with it: the order has one operative sentence and one sentence fixing its effective date. The revocation was exhausted when it took effect, May 4, 1939. No later instrument affecting this order was found in the held corpus. The held text is the machine-extracted text layer of the Federal Register issue (a recheck extraction); OCR wording remains subject to a page check against the PDF, which is not held.

savings.reason: The order has no savings or transition clause. The revocation changed the legal status of the port by ending its designation; that completed change, not any continuing command of this order, is the surviving consequence, and it is recorded as accrued. No held source shows any other residual effect.
